statement: In a calendar, the days of a month are written in rows of 7, from Monday to Sunday. This month has 31 days, and the 1st is a Wednesday. How many different 2 by 2 squares of four dates can be drawn on the calendar, with every box of the square holding a date?

choices.misconception: I counted 6 squares for each of the 4 pairs of neighbouring weeks, as if every week were complete.
I counted the squares between the full weeks but included only one of the two short weeks, $6 + 6 + 4$.
I counted 7 squares across each pair of weeks, one for each day, but a 2 by 2 square needs two neighbouring columns.
I only counted squares inside the three complete weeks and ignored both short weeks.

hints: Sketch the calendar and mark where the first and last weeks start and stop.

Counting by position: a 2 by 2 square is fixed by its top-left date. Count the possible top-left positions for each pair of neighbouring weeks separately, taking care with the short first and last weeks.
Week 1 is Wednesday to Sunday (1 to 5) and week 5 is Monday to Friday (27 to 31). Weeks 2, 3 and 4 are complete.

solutions.reliable: The weeks are: 1 to 5 (Wednesday to Sunday), 6 to 12, 13 to 19, 20 to 26 (complete), and 27 to 31 (Monday to Friday). A 2 by 2 square uses two neighbouring weeks and two neighbouring days, and every box must hold a date. Weeks 1 and 2 share the five days Wednesday to Sunday, giving 4 squares. Weeks 2 and 3: 7 days, giving 6 squares. Weeks 3 and 4: 6 squares. Weeks 4 and 5: Monday to Friday, 5 days, giving 4 squares. Total $4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 20$. The transferable idea: in sliding-window counting, label each window by its starting position and count the starting positions row by row.
solutions.elegant: Two neighbouring weeks that share $n$ days in a row give $n - 1$ squares, one for each pair of neighbouring days: $(5 - 1) + (7 - 1) + (7 - 1) + (5 - 1) = 20$.

whyOnTest: Sliding windows are counted by their starting position; the short first and last weeks are where careless counts go wrong.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
